newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's labour war mars rosier economic outlook.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's labour war mars rosier economic outlook.

text.p: The battle between South African business and labour over controversial planned labour legislation is hotting up with fresh strike plans posing a threat to improved economic fundamentals.

Hopes for a successful relaxation of exchange controls post July 1, after evidence of a slowdown in the economy, could pave the way for a cut in the country's punitively-high interest rates, analysts have speculated.
This view is reinforced by most recent inflation figures, which are now seen trending firmly downwards, and a drop in latest money supply and private credit extension figures.
But current controversy over labour legislation mars the improved economic picture.

The 1.9-million strong Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) last week threatened fresh national strikes and a series of labour action in various regions in August to force business to revise radically its position over employment laws.
Business and labour have clashed over the Basic Conditions of Employment Bill, which was approved by cabinet in April but still has to be passed by parliament.
Labour has accused business of wanting to uphold "apartheid legislation in the labour market," vowing that it will fight an ideological war to achieve its aims at all costs.

Business is concerned that Cosatu's demands, if implemented, will increase its costs and lead to increased rigidity of the labour market which, it argues, will strangle economic growth and the important goal of job creation.

Employer grouping Business South Africa (BSA) has said the proposed labour legislation should be delayed until after a presidential jobs summit, which government has scheduled for October, or passed without the disputed sections.
"We should first create jobs and then discuss changes to legislation that affect labour policy," BSA deputy president Leslie Boyd said recently.
Business is concerned about the bill's wide scope and provisions which could raise employment costs to the point of creating obstacles to new jobs.

The main areas of dispute centre on labour's demands for a 40-hour working week, six months maternity leave of which at least four are paid, double payment for Sunday work and no downward variation of basic conditions of employment.

"Cosatu's gripe is with employers not just with business and the biggest employer in the country is the state. Their primary fight is with the state and it has to be with the (government's) Growth, Employment and Redistribution (Gear) strategy itself," says industrial relations consultant Gavin Brown.
He says the important issue is the planned jobs summit in October.
"Job creation is the most important thing and it's the one are that's not happening in Gear."

Latest figures by the Central Statistical Services show that 71,000 jobs were shed in the non-agricultural formal sector lat year, dashing hopes that 126,000 jobs could be created, as envisaged in Gear.
Gear projected 126,000 new jobs for last year and 252,000 this year to help alleviate the country's chronic unemployment problem.
Syfrets economist Sandra Gordon says the issue of job creation is complex.
"Something needs to be done to help create employment of a longer-term nature but it's not like fiscal policy.
"We're heavily reliant on government, business and labour working together to try to create the right climate," she says.

Labour Minister Tito Mboweni says the need for a new legislation on minimum conditions and standard of work is unquestionable. At the same time, he says, there is a need to "resort to more direct policy instruments to generate employment."
To this end, government was finalising an employment strategy for debate at the jobs summit in October.
Brown says the planned labour legislation poses more obstacles to job generation.
"The lack of job creation is due to complex reasons but it's certainly not being helped by legislation that makes employment of people more expensive," he said.
-- Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
